questions.stem: Why must Sir Walter Elliot let Kellynch Hall to a tenant?
options: His eldest daughter has married, and the house passes to her husband
His health is failing, and his doctor orders him to live by the sea
His spending has left him in debt, so he must cut costs and move to Bath
His heir, Mr Elliot, demands to take over the house before he inherits it
questions.explanation: Sir Walter has lived beyond his means. Letting Kellynch and moving to cheaper lodgings in Bath is the only way to save money without giving up his pride entirely.

questions.stem: Who rents Kellynch Hall?
options: Admiral Croft and his wife, who is Captain Wentworth's sister
Captain Harville and his family, who are old friends of Anne's
Mr Elliot, the cousin who will one day inherit the baronetcy
Charles Musgrove and Mary, who move there from Uppercross
questions.explanation: The tenant is a naval officer, and his wife's brother is the man Anne once loved. The arrangement brings Wentworth back into Anne's world.

questions.stem: What happened between Anne and Frederick Wentworth eight years before the novel begins?
options: They were married, but Wentworth left her to go to sea
They quarrelled at a ball, and Anne refused to dance with him
They were close friends, but Wentworth never proposed
They were engaged, but Anne was persuaded to break it off
questions.explanation: Anne was nineteen and Wentworth a young officer with no fortune. Lady Russell persuaded her that the engagement was unwise, and Anne has regretted it ever since.

questions.stem: Why did Lady Russell advise Anne against the engagement?
options: Wentworth planned to take Anne away to live in the West Indies
Wentworth had no fortune or connections and an uncertain profession
Wentworth was known to drink and gamble away his naval pay
Wentworth was much older than Anne and settled in his ways
questions.explanation: Austen says he had 'nothing but himself to recommend him'. Lady Russell acted from love and prudence, which is why the novel does not make her a simple villain.

questions.stem: Where does Anne go while her father and sister settle in Bath?
options: To Uppercross, to stay with her younger sister Mary Musgrove
To Lyme, to stay with Captain and Mrs Harville by the sea
To London, to stay with Lady Russell for the whole winter season
To Kellynch Lodge, to keep house alone for Mr Shepherd
questions.explanation: Mary claims to be ill and wants company. At Uppercross Anne is useful to everyone and noticed by no one, and it is there that she meets Wentworth again.

questions.stem: Which young women does Wentworth pay attention to at Uppercross?
options: Henrietta Musgrove and Elizabeth Elliot, Anne's sister
Louisa and Henrietta Musgrove, Charles's sisters
Elizabeth Elliot and Mrs Clay, the Bath visitors
Louisa Musgrove and Mrs Smith, Anne's old friend
questions.explanation: Wentworth enjoys the lively Musgrove sisters, especially Louisa, and the families expect him to marry one of them. Anne must watch, believing he no longer cares for her.

questions.stem: What happens on the Cobb at Lyme?
options: Mr Elliot is thrown from his horse and badly injured
Mary slips into the sea and is rescued by Captain Benwick
Louisa jumps from the steps, falls and is knocked unconscious
Henrietta faints on the steps and is carried to the inn
questions.explanation: Louisa insists on being jumped down the steps a second time and falls. While others panic, Anne stays calm and gives directions, and Wentworth sees her worth again.

questions.stem: Whom does Louisa Musgrove become engaged to while she recovers at Lyme?
options: Mr Elliot, who stays at Lyme to visit her every afternoon
Charles Hayter, the cousin who had courted her sister
Captain Benwick, the grieving young officer who loves poetry
Captain Wentworth, who blames himself for her terrible fall at Lyme
questions.explanation: Benwick had been mourning his dead fiancée, Fanny Harville. The engagement frees Wentworth, who had felt bound to Louisa, and shows how quickly Benwick's grief fades.

questions.stem: What does Mrs Smith reveal about Mr Elliot?
options: He encouraged her husband's ruin and refused to help her as executor
He was once secretly engaged to Anne, years before Captain Wentworth was
He has lost his fortune and must marry money to pay his debts
He has gambled away the whole fortune of his late wife at cards
questions.explanation: Mrs Smith says Mr Elliot is 'a man without heart or conscience'. He led her husband into extravagance, then would not act for her when she was left poor and ill.

questions.stem: How does Wentworth finally declare his feelings to Anne?
options: He speaks to her at a concert after Mr Elliot leaves her side
He asks Lady Russell for permission to propose to her again
He sends a message through Admiral Croft asking her to meet him
He writes her a letter while he hears her talking with Captain Harville
questions.explanation: At the White Hart, Anne argues to Harville that women love longest. Wentworth, writing nearby, hears her and writes his own letter, then leaves it for her.

questions.stem: How does the novel end?
options: Anne marries Wentworth, and Sir Walter marries Mrs Clay
Anne marries Wentworth, and Mr Elliot goes off to London with Mrs Clay
Anne marries Mr Elliot, and Wentworth returns to sea alone
Anne refuses both men, and stays with Lady Russell at Kellynch
questions.explanation: Anne and Wentworth marry, this time with Lady Russell accepting him. Mr Elliot's plan collapses as Mrs Clay leaves with him, and Anne becomes a sailor's wife.

questions.stem: The novel moves from Kellynch and Uppercross to Lyme and then Bath. What is the main role of the Lyme chapters?
options: They are a flashback, where we see Anne's engagement eight years ago
They are the turning point, where Anne's calm judgement is seen by all
They are a comic interlude, easing the tension of the Uppercross chapters
They are the climax, where Wentworth finally admits that he still loves Anne
questions.explanation: At Lyme Louisa's fall tests everyone, and Anne is the one who keeps her head. Mr Elliot also first notices Anne there, so her 'bloom' and her value return together.

questions.stem: Sir Walter Elliot is best described as:
options: shy and bookish, caring most about his studies
stern and religious, caring most about his duty
vain and snobbish, caring most about rank and looks
kind and generous, caring most about his tenants' welfare
questions.explanation: Austen states that 'Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot's character'. He judges people by their titles and their complexions.

questions.stem: How is Anne treated by her own family at the start of the novel?
options: She is overlooked by her father and sister, who think her of no importance
She is spoiled by her father, who prefers her to her two sisters
She is consulted by her father, who trusts her advice on money matters
She is pitied by her father, who blames himself for her lost bloom
questions.explanation: To her father and Elizabeth, Anne 'was nobody'. Her quiet good sense goes unnoticed, which makes her later recognition more powerful.

questions.stem: Lady Russell is best described as:
options: a careless neighbour who never noticed Anne's feelings
a loving friend whose respect for rank and prudence misled her
a wise adviser whose judgement the novel fully endorses
a cold snob who cared little for Anne's happiness
questions.explanation: Lady Russell was Anne's mother's close friend and loves Anne deeply. Her mistake was to value fortune and position too highly, and she later admits she was wrong about both men.

questions.stem: Why does Anne distrust Mr Elliot even before Mrs Smith speaks?
options: He is poor and plainly hoping to marry her for her fortune
He is always polished and agreeable, but never open or warm
He is rude to her father and makes fun of her sister in public
He talks too freely, sharing every opinion and feeling at once
questions.explanation: Austen writes that he was 'rational, discreet, polished, but he was not open'. Anne values warmth and sincerity, which she sees in Wentworth and the naval families.

questions.stem: What does the marriage of Admiral and Mrs Croft show?
options: A secret unhappiness, as she longs to leave the navy behind her
An affectionate, equal partnership, as she has shared his life at sea
A cold arrangement for money, as they live in separate parts of the house
A warning against marrying young, as they quarrel at every meeting
questions.explanation: Mrs Croft has sailed with her husband and drives the gig with him. Their marriage models the companionship Anne hopes for.

questions.stem: Captain Benwick is introduced mourning his fiancée and quoting sad poetry. What does Anne advise him?
options: To write his own poems about his lost fiancée
To read more prose as well, to strengthen his mind
To give up the navy and find a quiet life on land instead
To return to Fanny's family and live with them
questions.explanation: Anne gently suggests a larger share of prose in his reading. The scene is comic and kind, and Benwick's quick move to Louisa questions how deep his grief went.

questions.stem: When was Persuasion published?
options: In 1811, as Austen's very first novel to be published
In 1813, just after Pride and Prejudice appeared
In 1830, edited by her nephew from her letters
In late 1817, after Jane Austen's death that year
questions.explanation: Austen died in July 1817. Persuasion appeared at the end of that year, published together with Northanger Abbey.

questions.stem: How had Wentworth made his fortune in the years since Anne refused him?
options: By trading in sugar and tea between England and the West Indies
By marrying a rich widow, who died soon after the wedding
By capturing enemy ships in the war, which earned prize money
By inheriting the estate of a wealthy uncle who died abroad
questions.explanation: Naval officers shared prize money for captured ships. Wentworth has made 'a handsome fortune' by his own efforts in the wars against Napoleon.

questions.stem: What social change does the novel suggest through Sir Walter and the navy?
options: The gentry are welcoming naval officers as their social equals
The old landed gentry is declining while men who rise on merit gain respect
The navy is losing its power while country estates are growing richer
Titles are becoming more important while merit counts for less and less
questions.explanation: Sir Walter is in debt and must rent out his estate, while the Crofts look after it better than he did. Austen contrasts inherited rank with worth earned through work.

questions.stem: Sir Walter's favourite book is the Baronetage, a record of titled families. What does this show?
options: His learning: he is writing a history of English titled families
His grief: he reads it to remember his late wife's family
His worry: he searches it for a titled match for Elizabeth
His vanity: he reads it for his own family's entry and his rank
questions.explanation: The novel opens with him reading his own family's page 'for his own amusement'. It is an ironic first picture of a man who cares only for rank.

questions.stem: In Bath, Sir Walter and Elizabeth are anxious to be recognised by their cousins, Lady Dalrymple and her daughter. What is Austen satirising?
options: Their loyalty, as they stand by family through hard times
Their shyness, as they are nervous of meeting new people in Bath
Their snobbery, as they chase titled relations of little real worth
Their kindness, as they visit poor relations in their small humble homes
questions.explanation: The Dalrymples have rank but little else to recommend them. Anne is embarrassed by the fuss, while her family neglect worthier people like Mrs Smith.

questions.stem: Which question is most central to Persuasion?
options: Can grief for a lost love ever truly be overcome in time?
Can a person ever change the class into which they were born?
When should we yield to others' advice, and when follow our own judgement?
Should a daughter obey her father in choosing whom to marry?
questions.explanation: Anne was persuaded once and suffered for it, yet she still thinks she was right to listen. The novel weighs firmness against open-mindedness throughout.

questions.stem: Wentworth praises firmness of mind to Louisa, but Louisa's fall at Lyme complicates this. How?
options: Her fall shows that firmness is the virtue Anne most needs to learn from Louisa
Her fall shows that Anne was wrong to listen to Lady Russell's advice
Her recovery shows that firmness is rewarded with good health and luck
Her stubborn insistence on jumping shows that firmness can become reckless
questions.explanation: Louisa's 'I am determined I will' leads straight to the accident. Wentworth learns that a persuadable, gentle mind like Anne's has its own strength.

questions.stem: How does the novel present constancy, or faithful love?
options: As a hopeless ideal, since Wentworth has long forgotten Anne
As Anne's quiet strength, tested over years and finally rewarded
As a weakness that keeps Anne from enjoying her life in Bath
As a virtue men show more than women, as Captain Benwick proves
questions.explanation: Anne has loved Wentworth for eight years. Her talk with Harville about who loves longest makes constancy the novel's climax, and Benwick's quick engagement undercuts any claim that men are more constant.

questions.stem: How is the story narrated?
options: In the third person, closely following Anne's thoughts and feelings
In the first person, by Anne writing letters to Lady Russell
In the first person, by Wentworth looking back on his courtship
In the third person, moving evenly between all the characters
questions.explanation: We see events largely through Anne's eyes, though the narrator also comments with irony. This lets us share her hidden pain while others ignore her.

questions.stem: 'Now they were as strangers; nay, worse than strangers, for they could never become acquainted.' Which technique does this sentence show?
options: Epistolary form, in which Anne writes her feelings in a letter
Omniscient summary, in which the narrator reports events coolly
Free indirect discourse, blending the narrator's voice with Anne's feeling
Dramatic monologue, in which Anne speaks her thoughts aloud on stage
questions.explanation: The words are the narrator's, but the bitterness is Anne's. Free indirect discourse lets Austen take us inside Anne's mind without leaving the third person.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the novel's opening, in which Sir Walter reads about himself in the Baronetage?
options: It satirises his vanity at once through the narrator's irony
It builds sympathy for him as a lonely, grieving widower
It creates mystery about a secret in the family's history
It shows his care for the family's history and its future
questions.explanation: A man whose only book is a list of his own family is ridiculous. Austen's dry irony tells us how to judge him before the plot begins.

questions.stem: Anne overhears Wentworth's speech to Louisa in the hedgerow, and later Wentworth overhears Anne talking with Harville. Why do these overheard moments matter?
options: They create comedy by catching characters out in small lies
They let characters learn true feelings that could not be said openly
They show that both characters are rude and listen at doors on purpose
They show how gossip spreads through the small world of the gentry
questions.explanation: Manners prevent open declarations, so feeling travels sideways. What Wentworth overhears at the White Hart finally prompts his letter.

questions.stem: Who writes 'You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.'?
options: Benwick, in a poem he writes about the late Fanny Harville
Mr Elliot, in a letter to Anne proposing marriage
Wentworth, in his letter to Anne at the White Hart
Anne, in a letter to Wentworth she never sends
questions.explanation: Wentworth writes this while overhearing Anne. The intense, broken style shows feeling bursting through the restraint he has kept for most of the novel.

questions.stem: Anne says the only privilege she claims for her sex is 'that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone.' Who is she speaking to, and why does it matter?
options: Louisa Musgrove, while warning her against Captain Benwick
Captain Harville, while Wentworth overhears her at his letter
Lady Russell, while explaining why she refused Charles Musgrove
Mrs Smith, while hearing the truth about Mr Elliot's character
questions.explanation: Anne is arguing about constancy, but she is also speaking of herself. Wentworth hears it and writes his letter, so her words bring about the ending.

questions.stem: 'She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older.' What does this sentence suggest about Anne?
options: Experience has taught her to value love above caution
Experience has taught her to value caution above love
She was naturally prudent and has stayed cautious since
She regrets learning romance and wishes she were prudent
questions.explanation: The narrator calls this 'the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning'. Anne was made cautious too young, and time has reversed it.

questions.stem: What does the narrator mean by 'her word had no weight' when describing Anne's place at home?
options: Her family think she speaks too much and want her to be quiet
Her family respect her advice, but cannot afford to follow it
Her family ignore her opinions and expect her always to give way
Her family think her still too young to judge for herself
questions.explanation: The passage ends, 'she was only Anne.' Her good sense is wasted on a vain family who do not value her.

questions.stem: Wentworth tells Louisa, 'It is the worst evil of too yielding and indecisive a character, that no influence over it can be depended on.' Why is this ironic?
options: He is really speaking of himself, yet he is the most decisive man in the novel
He is really mocking Captain Benwick, yet Benwick proves the most constant of men
He is really warning Louisa, yet she proves the most yielding of all
He is really thinking of Anne, yet Louisa's own stubbornness soon causes disaster
questions.explanation: Anne, listening, knows he means her yielding to Lady Russell. Louisa's fall at Lyme then shows the dangers of the firmness he praises.

questions.stem: Anne says of books that 'the pen has been in their hands'. What is her point?
options: Books are better evidence about love than personal experience
Books cannot be trusted on love because most of them are fiction
Books show women as fickle because men have written most of them
Books show women as constant because women have written most of them
questions.explanation: Harville cites books that call women changeable. Anne replies that men have had 'every advantage' in telling their own story, a sharp point about who controls the record.

questions.stem: Mary reports Wentworth's comment on Anne: 'You were so altered he should not have known you again.' What is its effect on Anne?
options: It amuses her, since she has not changed at all in the eight years
It wounds her, confirming that he no longer finds her attractive
It pleases her, since she hopes to begin again as a stranger
It angers her, since she knows Mary has invented the remark
questions.explanation: Anne believes her looks and his love have both faded. The remark marks how far apart they seem early in the novel, making the later reversal stronger.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the question 'Analyse how Austen presents the costs of persuasion in Persuasion.'?
options: Anne Elliot is the daughter of Sir Walter Elliot and lives at Kellynch Hall
Austen shows that yielding to Lady Russell cost Anne eight years of quiet suffering
Persuasion is a novel by Jane Austen that was published in 1817 after her death
This essay will analyse how Austen presents persuasion in the novel Persuasion
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence names the author, makes a claim that answers the question and points to evidence. The others give facts, announce or describe.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Louisa jumps off the Cobb and hits her head.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the people who were standing on the Cobb when Louisa fell down
Describe the journey back to Uppercross after the accident in detail
Explain how the fall exposes the danger of the firmness Wentworth praised
Add the exact height of the steps and the time of day the fall happened
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the event shows. Linking the fall to the novel's debate about firmness and persuasion makes it evidence for an argument.
